theorem.content:
\label{thm-KF}
Suppose that $K$ is a number field and $e$ a positive integer. For almost all $\sigma \in G_K^e$, any finite extension of $\overline{K}(\sigma)$ is both torally Kummer-faithful and AVKF, and thus, Kummer-faithful.
theorem.label: thm-KF

post_theorem_intro_text:
Notice that the absolute Galois group $G_{\overline{K}(\sigma)}$ of $\overline{K}(\sigma)$ is abelian when $e = 1$.
This immediately implies that the following corollary.
Actually, more is true: there are continuum many algebraic extensions of $K$ up to $K$-isomorphism which are Kummer-faithful fields with abelian absolute Galois group.
See Corollary~\ref{cor-continuummany} for details.

\begin{corollary}\label{cor-thm-KF}
Let $K$ be a number field.
There exists an algebraic extension of $K$ that is Kummer-faithful and has abelian absolute Galois group.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}
One of the assertions in Theorem~1.11 of Mochizuki's paper~\cite{Mochizuki15} claimed that the absolute Galois group of any Kummer-faithful field of characteristic zero is \textit{slim}, i.e., every open subgroup has trivial center.
He recently informed us that the proof of this assertion has a gap.
Corollary~\ref{cor-thm-KF} is incompatible with this assertion and shows the existence of a counterexample in the general case, but the proof is not constructive.
It also answers in the negative the questions~\cite[Remark~2.4.1, Questions~1 and~2]{MT} posed by Minamide and Tsujimura which asked whether the absolute Galois group of any torally Kummer-faithful field is slim.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}
The assertions related to the (torally) Kummer-faithfulness of $\overline{K}(\sigma)$ have appeared twice previously, first in~\cite[Corollary~1]{Ohtani22} and then in the PhD thesis~\cite[Theorem~4.2.1]{AsayamaThesis} of the author, but their proofs in both works were incorrect.
The former has been corrected and the weaker version~\cite[Corollary~1]{Ohtani23} was proved.
In our previous paper~\cite{AT}, the latter was addressed in p.~5 and the weaker result~\cite[Theorem~5.3]{AT} was shown.
\end{remark}

The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm-KF} is carried out by separating it into two parts; the torally Kummer-faithfulness part and the AVKF-ness part.
We provide proofs for each part in Sections~\ref{sec-TKFpart} and~\ref{sec-AVKFpart}, respectively.
The approaches to proving these parts are somewhat similar.
First, we reformulate the problem by reducing it to the calculation of measures.
For the AVKF-ness part, this step has been done by Jarden and Petersen~\cite{JP22}.
Then the calculation of measures is performed.
For the torally Kummer-faithfulness part, this step is based on a refinement of the proof of the weaker version~\cite[Theorem~5.3]{AT} presented in our previous paper.
Finally, we conclude the proof by using a combinatorial approach similar to that described by Zywina~\cite[pp.~495--496]{Zywina16} (see also~\cite[p.~49]{JP19}).
Section~\ref{sec-cor} contains corollaries to Theorem~\ref{thm-KF}.

theorem.content:
\label{thm:mainsplitting}
Let $G$ and $P$ be as above. Let $\Gamma<G$ be an irreducible lattice with finite center and set $\Lambda=\Gamma/Z(\Gamma)$. Let $({\mathcal N},\tau)$ be a trace-preserving $G$-von Neumann algebra, on which each $G_i$ acts ergodically and $Z(\Gamma)$ acts trivially. Then every von Neumann algebra $\mathcal{M}$ with
\[
\mathcal{N} \rtimes\Lambda\subset \mathcal{M} \subset (L^\infty(G/P, \nu_P) \overline{\otimes} \mathcal{N}) \rtimes \Lambda
\]
is a crossed product of the form $(L^\infty(G/Q, \nu_Q) \overline{\otimes} \mathcal{N}) \rtimes \Lambda$ for some $P<Q<G$.
theorem.label: thm:mainsplitting

ref_dict.thm:nciftfield:
\begin{thm}
\label{thm:nciftfield}
Let $(N, \tau)$ be a trace-preserving $G$-von Neumann algebra that is $G$-irreducible, i.e., $N$ is $H$-ergodic for every non-central normal subgroup $H<G$. Consider a $G$-invariant von Neumann subalgebra
\[
(N, \tau) \subseteq (M, \tau) \subseteq (N, \tau) \ \bar{\otimes} \ L^\infty(G / P, \nu_{P}),
\]
then
\[
(M, \tau) = (N, \tau) \ \bar{\otimes} \ L^\infty(G / Q, \nu_{Q})
\]
for some $G$-invariant subalgebra 
$L^\infty(G / Q, \nu_{Q}) \subseteq L^\infty(G / P, \nu_{P})$.
\end{thm}

sketch:
The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:mainsplitting} “relies on four main ingredients and essentially follows the same strategy employed in \cite{boutonnet2023noncommutative}.”

1. For $d\ge 2$, it “make[s] essential use of the notion of $G_i$–continuous elements” and “roughly speaking, we show that $G_i$-continuous elements remain invariant under tensoring by the tracial von Neumann algebra $({\mathcal N},\tau)$,” yielding that the subalgebra of $G_i$–continuous elements is $L^\infty(G_i/P_i,\nu_{P_i})$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:invarince undertensor}).

2. For $d=1$, one “need[s] a version of the non-commutative Nevo-Zimmer theorem” for higher-rank $k$-simple groups, obtained as a corollary of \cite[Theorem 5.4]{bader2023charmenability} (see Theorem~\ref{thm:mainembeddingprt}).

3. One then “pair[s] the analytic techniques of Suzuki~\cite{suzuki} along with the structural arguments of Bader–Boutonnet–Houdayer–Peterson~\cite {bader2022charmenability} to achieve the desired crossed-product rigidity,” adapting the Boutonnet–Houdayer strategy “to our purpose of providing ${\mathcal M}=\cM_0\rtimes \Lambda$.”

4. “Finally, the classification of the intermediate von Neumann algebra $\mathcal{M}$ now reduces to understanding the structure of the $\Gamma$-invariant coefficient subalgebra $\mathcal{M}_0$.” Using “the non-commutative versions of Bader-Shalom \cite{amrutam2025non} and Stuck-Nevo-Zimmer (see Theorem~\ref{thm:nciftfield}),” one shows every intermediate $\cM_0$ is of the form $\mathcal{M}_0=L^\infty(G/Q,\nu_Q)\overline{\otimes}\mathcal{N}$ for some $P<Q<G$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tensorproducts}), which yields the claimed classification of $\mathcal M$.

theorem.label: thm:main-intro

post_theorem_intro_text:
The estimate \eqref{eq:main} makes the exponential behavior transparent:
once $S$ contains many well-separated ``good'' vertices in the sense of the packing
definition, the probability that \emph{none} of $S$ connects to infinity decays exponentially
in the packing number.

\subsection{Method: FCA + functional characterization of $p^{\mathrm{site}}_{c}$}
The proof is based on an FCA mechanism:
\begin{itemize}
\item a \emph{functional} input: the local functional $\phi^{p}_{v}(S)$ from \cite{ZL24},
which characterizes $p^{\mathrm{site}}_{c}(G)$ through finite-volume connectivity data;
\item a \emph{cutset/local-boundary} step: for each chosen vertex, we compare
disconnection from infinity with disconnection from an inner boundary of a ball
(in an iteratively punctured graph);
\item an \emph{amplification} step: by selecting well-separated vertices (the packing),
we exploit independence to amplify a uniform positive probability of connection to infinity
into an exponential bound for the joint disconnection event.
\end{itemize}
In particular, the characterization theorem from \cite{ZL24} ensures that for $p>p^{\mathrm{site}}_{c}(G)$
one can find vertices whose local functionals are uniformly close to $1$ for \emph{all} finite
sets containing them as interior points; this yields a robust lower bound on the probability
of connecting to infinity and supplies the ``good'' vertices used in the packing construction.

The FCA mechanism was also used in \cite{ZL26} to establish the inequality
$p_u^{\mathrm{site}}(G)\ge 1-p_c^{\mathrm{site}}(G)$ for every infinite, connected, locally finite
planar graph $G$ whose set of end--equivalence classes (defined via a Freudenthal
embedding in $\mathbb S^2$) is countable.

\subsection{Organization}
Section~1 recalls the functional $\phi^{p}_{v}(S)$ and the characterization of
$p^{\mathrm{site}}_{c}(G)$ from \cite{ZL24}, introduces the $(p,\varepsilon,c)$--packing number,
and derives the quantitative bound \eqref{eq:main} from an induction-on-packing argument.
The amplification lemmas are presented in the same section, as they underpin both the packing
estimate and subsequent applications.

theorem.content:
Let $u$ be the unique solution of $(\ref{stoch. model})$ subjected to the homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions $(\ref{Neumann b.c.})$ and with a deterministic initial condition $u_{0} \in C(D)$. Then, the Malliavin derivative of $u(x,t)$ exists locally. Furthermore, for any $(x,t) \in D \times (0,T]$, the law of the random variable $u(x,t)$ is absolutely continuous
with respect to the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}$.

post_theorem_intro_text:
In Section \ref{Section 2}, we present some basic definitions from the theory of Malliavin calculus such as the notion of the Malliavin derivative, the spaces of random variables $\mathbb{D}^{1,2}$, $\mathbb{L}^{1,2}$ and their local versions $\mD_{\text{loc}}^{1,2}$, $\mL_{\text{loc}}^{1,2}$. Furthermore, we present the definition and some properties of our fractional noise as well as state the weak and mild formulation of the solution of $(\ref{stoch. model})$. 

In Section \ref{Section 3}, we provide some important estimates regarding the stochastic integral that appears in the mild formulation of the solution $u$ of $(\ref{stoch. model})$ (Lemma \ref{Estimates for stoch. int.}) and prove the space-time continuity of $u$ (Lemma \ref{continuity of u}). Moreover, we show that $u(x,t) \in \mD_{\text{loc}}^{1,2}$ by constructing a suitable localizing sequence $\{(\Omega_{n},u_{n}(x,t))\}_{n \in \mN_{*}}$. In particular, this construction involves the existence and uniqueness of an approximating sequence $\{u_{n}\}_{n \in \mN_{*}}$ that coincides with $u$ on $\Omega_{n}$ 
(Lemma \ref{main lemma 1}) and the representation of the Malliavin derivative of $u_n(x,t)$ (Lemma (\ref{main lemma 2})) both given as the solutions to specific integral equations. The Malliavin derivatives of $u(x,t)$ and $u_{n}(x,t)$ will then be directly correlated (see Remark \ref{important remark}).

In Section \ref{Section 4}, we present an important estimate involving the Malliavin derivative of $u_{n}(x,t)$ (Lemma \ref{important estimate}) that is then used to prove the absolute continuity of the law of $u_{n}(x,t)$ with respect to the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}$ (Lemma \ref{abs. con. of law of u_n}). Lastly, we show that this property of the law of $u_{n}(x,t)$ translates to the analogous property for the law of $u(x,t)$ (Theorem \ref{main theorem 2}) which in turn implies the existence of a density for $u(x,t)$.

As usual, the generic positive constant, depending on some parameter $T$ for example, will be denoted by $c(T)$ or simply $c$ if the dependence is not essential. Its exact value may also change from line to line. In many instances throughout this work, the symbols $\cdot, \diamond, \bullet$ will be used to represent the variables $x, y, s$ respectively, and will serve as placeholders within mathematical expressions, such as norms and operator actions.

    \arrow[d, shift left] 
& {(\mathcal{P}(Q),\, \varpi_{\mathcal{P}})} 
    \arrow[ld, "\mathcal{P}_p"'] 
    \arrow[rd, "\widetilde{\mathcal{P}_q}"] 
& {(G \ltimes \widetilde{G},\, \omega_2)} 
    \arrow[d, shift right] 
    \arrow[d, shift left] \\
\mathcal{A}(Q) 
& 
& 
\widetilde{G}
\end{tikzcd}
\]
To carry this out, we prove the following proposition in the appendix.
\begin{Proposition}
Suppose the Lie 2-group \(H\times H \rightrightarrows H\) has a Hamiltonian action on a symplectic groupoid \((\mathcal{G}, \omega) \rightrightarrows (M, \pi)\). Let \(x \in \mathrm{Lie}(H)^*\) be a regular value of the moment map \(\mu_M\), and let \((x,x) \in \mathrm{Lie}(H)^*\times \mathrm{Lie}(H)^*\) be a regular value of the moment map \(\mu_{\mathcal{G}}\). Assume the stabilizers of \(x\) and \((x,x)\) are \(H\) and \(H\times H\), respectively. If the actions of \(H\times H\) on \(\mu_{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}(x,x)\) and of \(H\) on \(\mu_M^{-1}(x)\) are both free and proper, then the quotient
\[
(\mathcal{G}//(H\times H), \omega_{\mathrm{red}}) \rightrightarrows (M//H, \pi_{\mathrm{red}})
\]
is a symplectic groupoid.
\end{Proposition}

theorem.content:
\label{thm:main}
Let $n(B)$ be the number of triples $u,v,w\in\mathbb{N}$ of square-full integers, such that $u+v=w$ and
$w\le B$. Then
\[n(B)\ll_\varepsilon B^{3/5-3/1555+\varepsilon}\]
for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$.
theorem.label: thm:main

ref_dict.thm2:
\begin{theorem}\label{thm2}
Let $a_1,a_2,a_3$ be non-zero square-free integers (of either sign) which are coprime in
pairs. Let $n(B;a_1,a_2,a_3)$ be the number of positive integer solutions
$x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2,y_3$ of the equation
\beql{axy}
a_1x_1^2y_1^3+a_2x_2^2y_2^3+a_3x_3^2y_3^3=0
\eeq
with $a_1y_1,a_2y_2$ and $a_3y_3$ square-free, and for which
\beql{range}
|a_1|x_1^2y_1^3,|a_2|x_2^2y_2^3,|a_3|x_3^2y_3^3\le B
\eeq
and
\beql{gcd}
\gcd(x_1y_1\,,\,x_2y_2\,,\,x_3y_3)=\gcd(a_1a_2a_3\,,\,x_1x_2x_3y_1y_2y_3)=1.
\eeq
Then $n(B;a_1,a_2,a_3)\ll_\ep B^{3/5-3/1555+\ep}$, for any fixed $\ep>0$.
\end{theorem}

post_theorem_intro_text:
The improvement, by $3/1555$, is disappointingly small. However it is hoped that the ideas in this
paper may inspire others to make more substantial progress now that an initial dent in the problem 
has been made.

Theorem \ref{thm:main} will be an easy consequence of the following result.
\begin{theorem}\label{thm2}
Let $a_1,a_2,a_3$ be non-zero square-free integers (of either sign) which are coprime in
pairs. Let $n(B;a_1,a_2,a_3)$ be the number of positive integer solutions
$x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2,y_3$ of the equation
\begin{equation}\label{axy}
a_1x_1^2y_1^3+a_2x_2^2y_2^3+a_3x_3^2y_3^3=0
\end{equation}
with $a_1y_1,a_2y_2$ and $a_3y_3$ square-free, and for which
\begin{equation}\label{range}
|a_1|x_1^2y_1^3,|a_2|x_2^2y_2^3,|a_3|x_3^2y_3^3\le B
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{gcd}
\gcd(x_1y_1\,,\,x_2y_2\,,\,x_3y_3)=\gcd(a_1a_2a_3\,,\,x_1x_2x_3y_1y_2y_3)=1.
\end{equation}
Then $n(B;a_1,a_2,a_3)\ll_\varepsilon B^{3/5-3/1555+\varepsilon}$, for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$.
\end{theorem}
To see how Theorem \ref{thm:main} follows from
Theorem \ref{thm2} suppose that $u+v=w$ with positive square-full integers $u,v,w$,
and let $h=\gcd(u,v,w)$. Then $h$ must be square-full, and $uh^{-1}$ must factor as $\prod p^e$
with $e\ge 2$ except possibly for primes $p| h$. Since every square-full integer may be 
written as a product $x^2y^3$ with $y$ square-free, we conclude that $u=ha_1x_1^2y_1^3$ for some 
integer $a_1|h$ coprime to $x_1y_1$, with $a_1y_1$ square-free. We may argue similarly for $v$ 
and $w$ and conclude that
\begin{eqnarray*}
n(B)&\le&\twosum{h\le B}{h\;\mathrm{square-full}}\sum_{a_1,a_2,a_3|h}n(B/h;a_1,a_2,a_3)\\
&\ll_\varepsilon&\twosum{h\le B}{h\;\mathrm{square-full}} \left(\frac{B}{h}\right)^{3/5-3/1555+\varepsilon}\tau(h)^3\\
&\ll_\varepsilon& B^{3/5-3/1555+\varepsilon},
\end{eqnarray*}
as required for Theorem \ref{thm:main}. Here $a_1,a_2,a_3$ are allowed to take both positive 
and negative values, and we use the fact that if $h$ runs over square-full
integers then $\sum_h h^{-\theta}<\infty$ whenever $\theta>\tfrac12$.
\bigskip

The main element in our strategy to prove Theorem \ref{thm2} is to consider the bi-homgeneous
congruence
\[a_1x_1^2y_1^3+a_2x_2^2y_2^3\equiv 0\; ( \text{mod} \; y_3^3).\]
After various manoeuvres we find that $(x_1,x_2,y_1,y_2)$ lies on one of a small number of lines
in $\mathbb{P}^3(\mathbb{Q})$ or, more precisely, on 2-dimensional lattices $\mathsf{M}\subset\mathbb{Z}^4$.
These produce equations of the shape 
\[F(u,v)=-a_3y_3^3\square,\]
where $F$ is a form of degree 5, and these are handled via the ``square-sieve''.  One needs to know 
about the size of $\det(\mathsf{M})$ for these lattices, which determines the range for the variables 
$u$ and $v$ above. Throughout these steps there are various special cases that arise which require
separate treatment.

One auxiliary result deserves mention here.
\begin{theorem}\label{cubic}
Let $\rho(B;a,b,c)$ be the number of integer solutions $x,y,z$ to the equation
\begin{equation}\label{ceq}
ax^3+by^3+cz^3=0
\end{equation}	
with $\gcd(x,y,z)=1$ and $\max(|x|,|y|,|z|)\le B$. Then
\[\rho(B;a,b,c)\ll_\varepsilon B^\varepsilon\]
for any $\varepsilon>0$, uniformly for all non-zero integer $a,b,c$.
\end{theorem}
It is clear from the proof that one may replace $B^\varepsilon$ by $B^{\varepsilon(B)}$ with some explicit function
$\varepsilon(B)$ tending to zero, but we shall not use this fact.  

For a general cubic form $C(x,y,z)$ with at least one non-trivial integral zero the corresponding 
counting function $\rho_C(B)$ will be asymptotically $c_B(\log B)^{r/2}$, where $r$ is the rank
of the Jacobian of $C$. It then follows that $\rho_C(B)\ll_{C,\varepsilon}B^\varepsilon$. It was shown by the author
\cite[Theorem 3]{HBcub} that one can remove the dependence on $C$ under a certain
``Rank Hypothesis''. This states that if $r(E)$ and $C_E$ denote the rank and conductor of an
elliptic curve $E$, then $r(E)=o(\log C_E)$. What is
special about our particular situation is that we can estimate the rank of the relevant elliptic curves
quite efficiently.

{\em Acknowledgement.} The author is particularly grateful to Tim Browning, for introducing 
him to this problem, explaining its background, providing references, and for pointing out
minor errors in an earlier draft of this paper.

theorem.content:
[Monotonicity]\label{monotonicity}
    For all $f \in \Rb\wspc{T}$, the function $x \mapsto f \circ x$ for $x \in \mathbb{U}^{>\mathbb{R}}$ is strictly increasing if $f' > 0$, strictly decreasing if $f' < 0$, and constant if $f' = 0$.
theorem.label: monotonicity

post_theorem_intro_text:
Since $\Rb\wspc{T}$ is generated from $T$, a naive proof by induction would be as follows: the conclusion is true for the base case $f = T$, $f = \log(T)$, \ldots; if $f = \sum_{i < \alpha} r_i e^{\gamma_i}$, we are free to assume the conclusion for each map $x \mapsto \gamma_i \circ x$, and we would like to deduce that $x \mapsto f \circ x$ is also monotonic. This works very well for $f \in \Jb_\mathfrak{O}^{>0}$, and we do so in \Cref{monotonicity-J}, but the inductive assumption falls short for the general case. We also need the following very weak form of mean value property: given $\gamma \in \Jb_\mathfrak{O}^{>0}$ and $x, y \in \mathbb{U}$ with $x > y > \mathbb{R}$, we have
\[ \frac{\gamma \circ x - \gamma \circ y}{x - y} \preceq \gamma' \circ y \quad \text{at least when} \quad \gamma \circ x - \gamma \circ y \preceq 1 \text{ or } (\gamma' \circ y)(x - y) \prec 1, \]
where $a \preceq b$ means $|a| \leq n|b|$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $a \prec b$ means $n|a| < |b|$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. The condition is almost trivial to verify in the base case of $T$, $\log(T)$, $\ldots$, as the associated functions $x \mapsto \log^{\circ n}(x)$ are all strictly increasing and \emph{concave}. The rest of the induction is then relatively straightforward (see \Cref{weak-mvp}), and it leads to a fairly short proof of \Cref{monotonicity}.

Since omega-series admit compositional inverses by~\cite{Bag2025}, namely for every $f \in \Rb\wspc{T}^{>\mathbb{R}}$ there is $g \in \Rb\wspc{T}^{>\mathbb{R}}$ such that $f \circ g = T$, we can immediately deduce the following.

\begin{maincor}\label{ivp}
    For all $f \in \Rb\wspc{T}$, the function $g \mapsto f \circ g$ for $g \in \Rb\wspc{T}^{>\mathbb{R}}$ has the intermediate value property: if $f \circ g \leq a \leq f \circ \tilde{g}$, there is $h \in \Rb\wspc{T}$ between $g$ and $\tilde{g}$ such that $f \circ g = a$.
\end{maincor}

$\mathrm{LE}$-series also admit compositional inverses within $\mathrm{LE}$ (\cite{DMM2001}), so the same holds for each $f \in \mathrm{LE}$ seen as a function from $\mathrm{LE}^{>\mathbb{R}}$ to $\mathrm{LE}^{>\mathbb{R}}$.

Given \Cref{monotonicity}, it also becomes relatively easy to prove the following form of Taylor's theorem. We write $a \asymp b$ to mean $a \preceq b$ and $b \preceq a$, and $O(b)$ to represent the set $\{a : a \preceq b\}$.

\begin{mainthm}[Taylor approximation for $\Rb\wspc{T}$]\label{taylor}
    Let $f \in \Rb\wspc{T}$ with $f \not\asymp T^k$ for any $k \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $x,\delta \in \mathbb{U}$ with $x > \mathbb{R}$ and $\delta \prec x$, $\frac{f' \circ x}{f \circ x}\delta \prec 1$. Then for all $n \geq 0$,
    \[ f \circ (x + \delta) = \sum_{i = 0}^n \frac{f^{(i)} \circ x}{i!}\delta^i + O\left((f^{(n+1)} \circ x)\delta^{n+1}\right). \]
\end{mainthm}

Other versions of the Taylor theorem exist in the literature, but they focus on the \emph{equality} $f \circ (x + \delta) = \sum_{i = 0}^\infty \frac{f^{(i)} \circ x}{i!}\delta^i$, which in general holds for a much smaller class of $\delta$'s (see for example~\cite[\S 6]{DMM2001},~\cite[Prop. 7.13]{BM2019}). What is notable here is that the Taylor approximation with error term is valid for the largest possible meaningful class of $\delta$'s. Indeed, when $\delta$ is small as required by \Cref{taylor}, the sequence $(f^{(n+1)} \circ x)\delta^{n+1}$ is \emph{strictly decreasing} for $\prec$, whereas as soon as $\delta$ is larger, then the sequence is \emph{weakly increasing}, making the error terms larger rather than smaller (see \Cref{radius-of-convergence}). In separate work with Bagayoko~\cite{BM2025}, we tackle the equality $f \circ (x + \delta) = \sum_{i = 0}^\infty \frac{f^{(i)} \circ x}{i!}\delta^i$ for omega-series, and show it holds provided $\delta$ is small in the sense of \Cref{taylor}, but with respect to every monomial appearing in $f$ rather than just $f$ itself, expanding and generalising the numerous existing variants of the same result.

Several questions remain open. Notably, while we have seen that omega-series and $\mathrm{LE}$-series, when interpreted as functions on their own positive infinite elements, have the intermediate value property, we are not claiming that they have the \emph{mean value property}: given $h$ such that $f' \circ h = \frac{f \circ g - f \circ \tilde{g}}{g - \tilde{g}}$, \Cref{monotonicity} does not seem to imply directly that $h$ is between $g$ and $\tilde{g}$. This may require a new argument.

Going beyond omega-series, it would be interesting to know if composition of elements in \emph{hyperserial fields} by \emph{hyperseries} (\cite{BHK2021}) is also monotonic as in \Cref{monotonicity}, and deduce the corresponding generalisation of \Cref{taylor}.

In this context, the first question is whether the weak mean value property used in the proof holds for the basic hyperlogarithmic monomials `$\ell_\alpha$', which represent, in a suitable sense, the `$\alpha$-th iterate of $\log$'. While the condition is satisfied locally, by the local Taylor expansion of the transfinite iterates of $\log$, it does not seem obvious at a first glance that it has to hold globally. For the usual $\log$, there is no issue because of the functional equation $\log(xy) = \log(x) + \log(y)$, but from $\ell_\omega$ onwards functions are less well behaved. In principle, this may require additional restrictions on the growth properties in the definition of hyperserial fields, and one should check if they are already satisfied in the surreal model of~\cite{BH2023}.

A similar, and potentially equivalent consideration emerges from \Cref{monotonicity-J} (monotonicity for $\gamma \in \mathbb{J}^{>0}$): its proof relies on the fact that for $x > y > \mathbb{R}$ and $z > w > \mathbb{R}$, if $y > w$ and $x - y > z - w$, then $\frac{\exp(x)}{\exp(y)} > \frac{\exp(z)}{\exp(w)} > 1$. Once again, this property seems easy to verify locally for transfinite iterations of $\exp$, but it is less clear whether it can be extended globally, due to the lack of a functional equation like $\exp(x + y) = \exp(x)\exp(y)$.

\subsection*{Acknowledgements} I thank Dino Peran, Jean-Philippe Rolin, and Tamara Servi for inviting me to work on normal forms. \Cref{taylor} was formulated only after it was clear it was the right statement to work with general omega-series. I also thank Vincent Bagayoko for the numerous helpful discussions on transseries and hyperseries, and for this note in particular, for helping me clarify that the bounds in \Cref{taylor} are sharp. Part of this research was carried out while the author was at the IHP trimester `Model theory, combinatorics and valued fields' in 2018 with support from the \foreignlanguage{french}{Fondation Sciences Mathématiques de Paris-FSMP}. The author was also supported by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council grant EP/T018461/1.

theorem.content:
\label{thm:key}
Fix $\varepsilon>0$. For any sequence of sites $i(n)\in \mathbb Z$ with
\[
|i(n)|\leq \frac{1}{2}\bigl(1-\varepsilon\bigr)n,
\]
we have
\[
\bP_n\bigl(\eta(i(n))=\mathfrak{s}\bigr) = \rho_c + o(1)\quad \text{as } n\to\infty,
\]
where $\eta\sim\bP_n$ is the final sleeping configuration of point-source ARW started from $n\delta_0$.
theorem.label: thm:key

post_theorem_intro_text:
\noindent As a consequence of our methods, specifically those in Section~\ref{sec:IDLA}, we obtain that the limiting critical measure, if it exists, is shift invariant.

\begin{prop}\label{cola}
Let $\alpha$ be a probability measure on $\{0,\mathfrak{s}\}^{\mathbb Z}$ which is a subsequential limit of the point-source laws $\bP_n$. Then $\alpha$ is shift invariant.
\end{prop}

To summarize, we find that for every fixed site $i\in\mathbb Z$ the one-site marginals $\bP_n|_{\{i\}}$ converge and the limiting probability that $i$ contains a sleeping particle is $\rho_c$. In particular, if the full microscopic limit measure $\alpha$ exists, it must be shift-invariant with average particle density $\rho_c$. These results confirm part of Conjectures 3--5 of~\cite{LevineSilvestriUniversality24}.

\subsection{Outline and Overview}
For $i\in\mathbb Z$, let $S_i:=\{\eta^{(n)}(i)=\mathfrak{s}\}$ be the event that site $i$ contains a sleeping particle in the final stabilized configuration. Equivalently, if $\eta\sim\bP_n$, then $S_i=\{\eta(i)=\mathfrak{s}\}$ and
\[
\bP_n\bigl(\eta(i)=\mathfrak{s}\bigr)=\mathbb P(S_i).
\]
The idea of the proof is to show that (1) the function $i\mapsto \bP_n(\eta(i)=\mathfrak{s})$ is relatively flat, and (2) that over any block of size $\omega(1)$ as $n \to \infty$, the particle density is close to $\rho_c$. We prove (1) in Section \ref{sec:IDLA} using a coupling between two instances of internal diffusion limited aggregation (IDLA), which can be thought of as ARW with infinite sleep rate. (2) is proved in Section \ref{sec:block} by an application of the machinery of~\cite{HoffmanJohnsonJunge24}, in combination with a semi-artificial toppling sequence involving IDLA on the $\omega(1)$-sized block. The artificial topplings allow us to give an upper bound on the probability that the particle density in the block is atypical. These two uses of IDLA are distinct and different from those in the existing ARW literature. Finally, in Section \ref{sec:complete} we combine (1) and (2) with elementary inequalities to obtain Theorem \ref{thm:key}.

theorem.content:
\label{main1}
Let $\Gamma\subset {\rm SO}(4)$ be one of the following finite subgroups:
$\{e\}$, the quaternion group $Q_8$, the prism group $D_{4n}$, the tetrahedral $T_{24}$, the octahedral $O_{48}$,
or the icosahedral $I_{120}$, where $n\in\mathbb{N}$.
Assume that the induced action of $\Gamma$ on $S^3$ is free, and set $M:=S^3/\Gamma$.
Let $v$ denote the $3$-form on $M$ induced by the standard volume form on $S^3$.

Then $H_3^{\rm gr}\bigl(\Diff_v(M)\bigr)$ contains a subgroup isomorphic to ${\Bbb Q}/{\Bbb Z}$.
theorem.label: main1

\begin{defn}\label{asfa} 
Fix $q \in \N$.
Let $\GG$ be a (Fr\'echet) Lie group.
A sequence of open subsets $\Ss=\{ S_n \subset \GG^{n+1}\}_{n \in \N }$ is said to be
\emph{well-configured (of length $q$)} if it satisfies the following conditions.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item (Simplicial condition) Each $S_n$ is closed under the diagonal action of $\GG$ and under the face maps, that is,
      $d_{i}^n(S_n) \subset S_{n-1}$ for any $0 \le i \le n$, and we have $S_0=\GG$.
\item For each $n$, let $\Z\langle S_n\rangle$ be the free $\Z$-module with basis $S_n$, and $\varepsilon:\Z\langle S_0\rangle\to\Z$ be the usual augmentation map.
      The augmented chain subcomplex of free $\Z[\GG]$-modules
      \[\Z\langle S_q\rangle
        \xrightarrow{ \ \partial_q \ }\Z\langle S_{q-1}  \rangle
        \xrightarrow{ \ \partial_{q-1} \ }
         \cdots 
        \xrightarrow{\ \partial_2 \ } \Z\langle S_1\rangle
        \xrightarrow{ \ \partial_1 \ } \Z\langle S_0\rangle
        \xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon \ } \Z \longrightarrow 0,
      \]
is required to be exact (equivalently, $H_n(\Z\langle S_*\rangle)=0$ for all $1 \leq n < q$ and $H_0(\Z\langle S_*\rangle)\cong \Z$).
\end{enumerate}
\end{defn}

\begin{thm}\label{main3}
Let $\C P^n$ be equipped with the symplectic $2$-form $\ww_n$ arising from the Fubini--Study metric.
Then the third group homology with integer coefficients of each of the following groups
contains a subgroup isomorphic to $\Q/\Z$:
\[
\Diff_{\ww_1}(\C P^1),\qquad
\Diff_{\ww_1\times \ww_1}(\C P^1\times \C P^1),\qquad
\Diff_{\ww_2}(\C P^2).
\]
\end{thm}

\begin{prop}\label{baas}
Let $G$ be a Fr\'echet--Lie group which is $(q-1)$-connected and assume that $\pi_q(G)$ is
finitely generated.
Fix $U:=U_{q+1}$ instead of $U_1$ and the filling $\{ \sigma_i\}_{i=0}^{q+1}$ on $\Ss_{G,U}$ as in
Subsection~\ref{sec223344}.

\smallskip
\noindent\textup{\emph{(I)}}
There exist smooth maps $c_1,\dots,c_m:S^q\to G$ such that the classes
$\{[c_1],\dots,[c_m]\}$ generate $\pi_q(G)$, and there exist $q$-cycles
$\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_m\in \Z\langle S_{q,G,U}\rangle$ with $\partial_q \gamma_\ell=0$
such that $\sigma_q(\gamma_\ell)\in C_q(G)$ represents the Hurewicz image of $[c_\ell]$.
In particular, the classes $[\sigma_q(\gamma_1)],\dots,[\sigma_q(\gamma_m)]$ generate $H_q(G)$.

Moreover, the kernel of
$\partial_q:\Z\langle S_{q,G,U}\rangle\to\Z\langle S_{q-1,G,U}\rangle$
is generated as a $\Z[G]$-module by $\Im(\partial_{q+1})$ and by the finitely many cycles
$\{\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_m\}$.

\smallskip
\noindent\textup{\emph{(II)}}
Let $\lambda\in\AAA^q(G)^G$ be a closed $G$-invariant $q$-form and let
$\Lambda\subset\R$ be a discrete subgroup such that
$\int_{\sigma_q(\gamma_\ell)}\lambda\in\Lambda$ for all $\ell$.
Then the associated cochain
$\mathcal F_{\sigma}(\lambda):S_{q,G,U}\to\R/\Lambda$ is a locally smooth
$G$-invariant group $q$-cocycle on the configured sequence $\Ss_{G,U}$.
\end{prop}
ref_dict.hyp11:
\begin{cor}\label{asaasa}
Let $M=S^3 /\Gamma$ be a spherical space form as above.
Then there exists a locally $C^{\infty}$ group $3$-cocycle $ \Diff_{v}(M)^4 \ra \R/\Z$
whose restriction to ${\rm Isom}^+(M)$ is cohomologous to the Chern--Simons cocycle.
\end{cor}
A result of a similar claim appears in \cite[Theorem~6.6]{Rez}, but there only the
existence of the cocycle is deduced in an abstract way using Quillen $K$-theory, and no statement
about local smoothness is given.
Moreover, in the case $\Gamma \neq 1$, the proof in \cite{Rez} predates the solution of the
generalized Smale conjecture and contains a gap.

\subsection{The hyperbolic case}\label{hyp11}

Incidentally, in constast to spherical geometry, we briefly explain how the same method yields group 3-cocycles in the
hyperbolic case.

\begin{prop}\label{hypc} 
Let $M$ be a closed hyperbolic $3$-manifold and let $v$ be the associated hyperbolic
volume 3-form.
Then there exists an $\R$-valued locally smooth $3$-cocycle $ (\Diff_{v}(M))^4 \longrightarrow \R.$
\end{prop}
\begin{proof}
By Mostow--Prasad rigidity, the composite
$\Isom^+(M)\hookrightarrow \Diff_v(M)\twoheadrightarrow \pi_0(\Diff_v(M))$
is an isomorphism and $\Isom^+(M)$ is finite.
By Gabai's hyperbolic Smale conjecture, the inclusion $\Isom^+(M)\hookrightarrow \Diff_v(M)$ is a homotopy equivalence.
Hence $\Diff_{v,0}(M)$ is contractible and $\Diff_v(M)\cong \Diff_{v,0}(M)\rtimes \Isom^+(M)$.

Let $p:\GG_M\to \Diff_{v,0}(M)$ be the universal cover. Then $\GG_M$ is contractible, in particular $2$--connected.
In particular $\pi_3(\Diff_{v,0}(M))=0$, so in Proposition~\ref{baas} there are no generators $\gamma_\ell$ in degree $3$. 

Choose $U$ and the affine filling $\sigma$ on $\Ss_{\GG_M,U}$ as in Subsection~\ref{sec223344}.
Applying the construction of Section~\ref{secDiff0Configured} with $\Lambda=\{0\}$ to the invariant form
$p^*\lambda_M=p^*q_M^*(v)$ produces a locally smooth $\R$--valued $3$--cocycle on $\GG_M$.
Since $\Isom^+(M)$ is finite, the standard transfer/averaging (cf.\ Lemma~\ref{321a}) yields an $\Isom^+(M)$--invariant class
and hence a locally smooth $\R$--valued $3$--cocycle on $\Diff_v(M)\cong \Diff_{v,0}(M)\rtimes \Isom^+(M)$.
\end{proof}

It would be very interesting to understand whether this cocycle is null cohomologous. If one could find a $3$-cycle
$\kappa\in H_3^{\rm gr}(\Diff_v(M) )$ satisfying nontriviality of the pairing $ \bigl\langle \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}(p^*(v)), \kappa \bigr\rangle \neq 0,
$
it would follow that $H_3^{\rm gr}(\Diff_v(M) )$ contains a copy of $\Z$.
The existence of such a $\kappa$ is left as a question for future work.

\subsection{Motivation: why configuration complexes are needed}\label{sec293392}

In this final subsection, as an extra note, we explain one of the motivations for introducing the
well-configured complex (Definition \ref{asfa}).
Roughly speaking, Cheeger--Chern--Simons type $\R/\Z$-valued cocycles are often
invisible to ordinary smooth cohomology on the full homogeneous complex
$\{\GG^{n+1}\}$. 

\begin{prop}\label{fass} 
Let $M=S^{4n-1}$ be the $(4n-1)$-sphere.
Let $\GG$ be a Fr\'echet--Lie subgroup of $\Diff^+(S^{4n-1})$ which contains the
subgroup ${\rm SO}(4n)$, and let $ \iota: {\rm SO}(4n)\hookrightarrow \GG $ be the inclusion.
Then, there is no smooth $\R/\Z$-valued $(4n-1)$-cocycle $\phi:\GG^{4n}\to\R/\Z$ such that the restriction
$\iota^*(\phi)\in H^{4n-1}_{\rm sm}({\rm SO}(4n);\R/\Z)$ is cohomologous to the CCS $(4n-1)$-cocycle in Example~\ref{ex21}. 
\end{prop}

\begin{proof}
Suppose such a cocycle $\phi$ exists.
The group $\pi_1({\rm SO}(4n))$ is annihilated by multiplication by $2$, and by the van
Est theorem we have $H^*_{\rm sm}({\rm SO}(4n);\R)=0$.
Hence, by Lemma~\ref{asfx} below, the class $2\,\iota^*(\phi)$ is trivial in
$H^{4n-1}_{\rm sm}({\rm SO}(4n);\R/\Z)$.
However, it is well known that the Chern--Simons invariant of odd-dimensional lens
spaces is nontrivial, and in particular no nonzero integer multiple of the CCS $(4n-1)$-cocycle is null-cohomologous.
This is a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{rem}\label{4433}
Proposition \ref{fass} might be known, since \cite[Theorem~6.6]{Rez2} is a similar statement. However, it is one of the reasons why we introduced the case
$\Ss\neq\{\GG^{n+1}\}_{n\in \N}$ in this paper.
Indeed, the problem ``to find a well-configured sequence $\Ss$ and a cocycle which is
smooth on $\Ss$'' is much more flexible and better suited for the study of group
cohomology than the rigid requirement of using the full homogeneous complex.
\end{rem}

\begin{lem}\label{asfx} 
Let $\GG$ be a connected Fr\'echet--Lie group such that $\pi_1(\GG)$ is finite.
If $H^m_{\rm sm}(\GG;\R)=0$, then every smooth class in $H^m_{\rm sm}(\GG;\R/\Z)$ is
annihilated by $|\pi_1(\GG)|$.
\end{lem}

\begin{proof}
Write $n_{\GG}=|\pi_1(\GG)|\in\N$.
Let $\phi : \GG^{m+1} \to \R/\Z$ be a smooth group $m$-cocycle.
It suffices to show that $n_{\GG}\phi$ is null-cohomologous.

The map $\R/\Z \to \R/\Z$, $x \mapsto n_\GG x$ induces multiplication by $n_{\GG}$ on
$\pi_1(\R/\Z)$.
Hence the induced map $ ( n_{\GG} \circ \phi )_* : \pi_1(\GG^{m+1}) \to \pi_1(\R/\Z)$
is the zero map, so $n_{\GG}\circ\phi$ lifts to a smooth map $
 \Phi : \GG^{m+1} \ra \R. $ Notice that $\Phi$ is invariant under the diagonal action of $\GG$.
Indeed, for $g \in \GG$, the difference $g^*\Phi - \Phi$ is a $\Z$-valued smooth function; hence it is constant, and substituting $g=e$ shows that this constant must be
$0$. 
Thus $g^*\Phi=\Phi$ for all $g \in \GG$.

Next, we show that $\Phi$ is an $m$-cocycle.
The coboundary $\partial^m(\Phi) : \GG^{m+2} \to \R$ is continuous and $\Z$-valued, hence
constant; denote this constant by $c \in \Z$.
If $m$ is even, then $\partial^m(\Phi)(e,\dots,e)=0$, so $\partial^m(\Phi)=0$ and $\Phi$
is an $m$-cocycle.
If $m$ is odd, then $\Phi -c$ is an $m$-cocycle.
In either case, since $H^m_{\rm sm}(\GG;\R)=0$, there exists a smooth
$(m-1)$-cochain $\eta : \GG^m \to \R$ such that $\partial^{m-1}(\eta)=\Phi-c$.
Let $\pi : \R \to \R/\Z$ be the natural projection.
Then, $ \partial^{m-1}(\pi \circ \eta) = \pi\circ\partial^{m-1}(\eta)
 = \pi\circ(\Phi-c) = n_\GG\,\phi.$ So $n_\GG\phi$ is a coboundary.
\end{proof}

\begin{rem}\label{asfaz}
The finiteness of $\pi_1(G)$ is essential.
For example, if $G=\R/\Z$, the universal coefficient theorem 
implies 
$H^1_{\rm gr}(\R/\Z ,\R/\Z) \cong \Hom(\R/\Z ,\R/\Z )$ and the map
\[
 \phi:G \times G  \longrightarrow \R/\Z,\qquad (g,h)\longmapsto g-h
\]
is a nontrivial smooth $1$-cocycle.
As a consequence, when $G=(\R/\Z)^n$, the cross product $\phi^{\times n}$ gives a
nontrivial smooth $n$-cocycle.
\end{rem}

\begin{exa}\label{lens}
Let $G$ be either $\SU(2)$ or $\SL_2(\C)$. 
In Example~\ref{ex23} we pointed out that a CCS cocycle can be realized as a smooth map $C_3^{\neq h}(G) \to\C/\Z$ on the subcomplex \eqref{989796}. 
However, by the same discussion of Lemma \ref{asfx}, this cocycle cannot be represented by wholly a smooth cocycle $G^4 \to \C/\Z$.  
\end{exa}

\section{Configured $3$-cocycles on groups of symplectomorphisms}\label{sec32884}

Throughout let $(M,\omega)$ be a closed $2n$-dimensional symplectic manifold, and let
$\Diff_{\omega}(M)$ be the group of symplectomorphisms of $(M,\omega)$, with identity
component $\Diff_{\omega,0}(M)$.
In Section \ref{sec3ss2884} , we construct a natural $\Diff_{\omega}(M)$-invariant Lie algebra $3$-cocycle and explain
how, under suitable geometric hypotheses, it gives rise to a locally smooth group
$3$-cocycle on a covering of $\Diff_{\omega,0}(M)$ via a well-configured complex.
In Section \ref{sec3sdds2884}, we prove Theorem~\ref{main3}.

\subsection{Invariant $3$-forms on $\Diff_{\omega}(M)$}\label{sec3ss2884}

We recall the basic Hamiltonian formalism (see, e.g., \cite{Can}).
Given $f\in C^\infty(M)$, the corresponding Hamiltonian vector field $X_f\in\mathfrak{X}(M)$
is defined by $  \iota_{X_f}\omega = - df,$ 
where $\iota$ denotes interior multiplication.
The Poisson bracket of $f,g\in C^\infty(M)$ is given by
$ \{f,g\} := \omega(X_f,X_g) = X_f(g)\in C^\infty(M).$
With this bracket $C^\infty(M)$ becomes a (topological) Lie algebra.
Let $\R_{\rm const}$ be the subalgebra consisting constant functions. 
We set 
\[
  \mathfrak{ham}(M,\omega)
  := \{ X_f \in \mathfrak{X}(M) \mid \iota_{X_f}\omega=-df,\ f\in C^\infty(M)\}
\]
for the Lie algebra of Hamiltonian vector fields.
Then the correspondence $
 f\ra X_f $
induces a Lie algebra isomorphism $C^\infty(M)/\R_{\rm const} \cong \mathfrak{ham}(M,\omega)$.

Next, we recall the known exact sequence \eqref{fffo} and show Lemma \ref{asax}. By Cartan's formula, $  L_X\omega = d(\iota_X\omega)$
for every $X\in\mathfrak{X}(M)$.
For $X\in\mathfrak{X}(M)$ with $ L_X\omega=0 $, put
$  \kappa  (X) := [\iota_X\omega] \in H^1(M;\mathbb{R}).
$
Then
\begin{equation}\label{fffo}
  0 \longrightarrow
  \mathfrak{ham}(M,\omega)
  \longrightarrow
  \{ X\in\mathfrak{X}(M) \mid L_X\omega=0\}
  \xrightarrow{\ \kappa \ }
  H^1(M;\mathbb{R})
  \longrightarrow 0
\end{equation}
is exact.
In addition, we now record an elementary identity, which might be known.
\begin{lem}\label{asax}
For $f,g\in C^\infty(M)$ define $ \langle f,g\rangle_M := \int_M f g\,\omega^n.$
Then for all $f,g,h\in C^\infty(M)$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ad-invariance-lemma}
  \langle \{f,g\},h\rangle_M
  + \langle g,\{f,h\}\rangle_M
  = 0. 
\end{equation}
\end{lem}

\begin{proof}
Liouville's theorem gives $L_{X_f}\omega^n=0$ for every $f$.
Hence, for any $\varphi\in C^\infty(M)$,
\[
  L_{X_f}(\varphi\,\omega^n )
   = X_f(\varphi)\,\omega^n  + \varphi\,L_{X_f}\omega^n 
   = X_f(\varphi)\,\omega^n.
\]
By Stokes' theorem and the compactness of $M$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{dddd}
 \int_M X_f(\varphi)\,\omega^n 
   = \int_M L_{X_f}(\varphi\,\omega^n )
   = \int_M d\bigl(\iota_{X_f}(\varphi\,\omega^n )\bigr)
   = 0.
\end{equation}
Now we will show \eqref{eq:ad-invariance-lemma} as
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \langle \{f,g\},h\rangle_M
  + \langle g,\{f,h\}\rangle_M
  &= \int_M \{f,g\}\,h\,\omega^n 
     + \int_M g\,\{f,h\}\,\omega^n  \\
 = \int_M \bigl(X_f(g)\,h + g\,X_f(h)\bigr)\,\omega^n   &= \int_M X_f(gh)\,\omega^n = 0,
\end{aligned}
\]
where we used \eqref{dddd} with $\varphi=gh$.
\end{proof}

In general, for a quadratic Lie algebra $(\mathfrak{g},[\ ,\ ],\langle\ ,\ \rangle)$ one defines the
alternating trilinear form
\begin{equation}\label{phiphi} 
  \Phi(x,y,z) := \langle x,[y,z]\rangle,\qquad x,y,z\in\mathfrak{g}.\end{equation} 
It is well known that $\Phi\in C^3_{\rm GF}(\mathfrak g;\R)$ is a Lie algebra
$3$-cocycle, which is called {\it the Cartan $3$-cocycle}; see, e.g., \cite[\S 4]{FSS}.
Especially, when $\g$ is a finite-dimensional simple Lie algebra and
$\langle\ ,\ \rangle$ is the Killing form, $H^3_{\rm GF}(\g;\R)\cong\R$ is generated by
the class of $\Phi$.

We now adapt this construction to the symplectic situation.
\begin{defn}\label{def:betaM}
Let $(M,\omega)$ be a compact symplectic manifold.
We define a 3-form $\beta_M$ as follows: 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-betaM}
 \beta_M \colon
\Lambda^3 \mathfrak{ham}(M,\omega)   \ra \mathbb{R}; \qquad  X_f\wedge X_g \wedge X_h
 \mapsto 
\frac{3}{ \pi^3 }  \langle f,\{g,h\}\rangle_M
   = \frac{3}{ \pi^3 } \int_M f\{g,h\}\,\omega^n.
\end{equation}
Here, $\beta_M$ does not depend on the choices of $f,g,h$ by the above $C^\infty(M)/\R_{\rm const} \cong \mathfrak{ham}(M,\omega)$,
and the coefficient $3/\pi^3$ is due to the normalization for $\Lambda =\Z$; see Lemma \ref{ddddd} later.
\end{defn}

By construction, $\beta_M$ is smooth and invariant under the diagonal action of
$\Diff_{\omega}(M)$ on $\mathfrak{ham}(M,\omega)$, and Lemma~\ref{asax} shows that
$\beta_M$ is a Lie algebra $3$-cocycle.
Thus $\beta_M$ defines a cohomology class
$ [\beta_M]\in H^3_{\rm GF}(\mathfrak{ham}(M,\omega);\R). $ 
In particular, if $H_1(M;\R)=0$, then \eqref{fffo} yields the identification
\begin{equation}\label{mm}
 \mathfrak{ham}(M,\omega)
 =
 \{ X\in\mathfrak{X}(M) \mid L_X\omega=0\},
 \end{equation} 
the full Lie algebra of symplectic vector fields.
In this case we may regard $\beta_M$ as a left-invariant closed $3$-form on the
symplectic diffeomorphism group $\Diff_{\omega}(M)$.

We now explain how $\beta_M$ gives rise to a locally smooth group $3$-cocycle via a
well-configured complex, under an explicit hypothesis on the periods of $\beta_M$.
\begin{prop}\label{444}
Let $M$ be a compact symplectic manifold such that $H_1(M;\R)=0$, and let
$\GG\to\Diff_{\omega,0}(M)$ be a covering group whose Lie algebra is
$\mathfrak{ham}(M,\omega)$.
Assume that $\GG$ is $2$-connected, and that $\GG$ and a discrete lattice $\Lambda \subset \R$ satisfy the same assumption as in Proposition~\ref{baas}~(II) for the closed $3$-form $\beta_M$.

Choose an identity neighbourhood $U\subset \GG$ and the corresponding sequence of \emph{$U$-small tuples} $S_{n,\GG,U}$ as in Lemma~\ref{key3}, and let $\sigma$ be the filling from Subsection~\ref{sec223344}.
Then the associated cochain
\[
\mathcal{F}_{\sigma}(\beta_M): S_{3,\GG,U} \longrightarrow \R/\Lambda
\]
defines a locally smooth $3$-cocycle on the configured complex $\Z\langle S_{*,\GG,U}\rangle$.
Furthermore, if $[\beta_M]\neq 0$ in $H^3_{\rm GF}(\mathfrak{ham}(M,\omega);\R)$, then the resulting
class $[ \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}(\beta_M)]$ is not zero in $H^3_{\rm loc,sm}(\GG;\R/\Lambda)$.
\end{prop}

\begin{proof}
By assumption, $\beta_M$ is a closed $\GG$-invariant $3$-form on $\GG$.
Since $\GG$ is $2$-connected, Lemma~\ref{key3} (with $q=3$) shows that the $U$-small sequence $S_{n,\GG,U}$ is well-configured of length $3$, and Subsection~\ref{sec223344} furnishes an filling $\sigma$ on it.
Applying Proposition~\ref{baas}~\textup{(II)} with $q=3$ and $\lambda=\beta_M$, we obtain a locally smooth
$\R/\Lambda$-valued $3$-cocycle $\mathcal{F}_{\sigma}(\beta_M)$ on $S_{3,\GG,U}$, which vanishes on $3$-cycles in $\Z\langle S_{3,\GG,U}\rangle$.
Finally, the last claim follows from Proposition~\ref{43333}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Proof of Theorem \ref{main3}}\label{sec3sdds2884}

We now specialize to projective spaces and prove Theorem~\ref{main3}.
Let $M=\C P^n$ and let $\omega_n$ be the Fubini--Study symplectic form with normalization $\int_{\C P^1}\omega_n =2\pi $.
Since the action of ${\rm PSU}(n+1)$ on $\C P^n$ preserves $\omega_n$, we have an inclusion $i_n: {\rm PSU}(n+1)\hookrightarrow \Diff_{\omega_n}(\C P^n)$. 
We begin by understanding the restriction of $\beta_M$ to ${\rm PSU}(n+1) $.

\begin{lem}\label{ddddd}
Let $M=\C P^n$ with the Fubini--Study symplectic form $\omega_n$, with the inclusion $i_n: {\rm PSU}(n+1)\hookrightarrow \Diff_{\omega_n}(\C P^n)$. 
Then the restriction $i_n^*(\beta_M)$ represents a nontrivial class in
$H^3_{\rm GF}(\mathfrak{psu}(n+1);\R)$.
Moreover,  if $n=1$, then $i_1^*(\beta_M) $ is equal to the ${\rm SO}(3)$-invariant volume form $ v_{ \R P^3} $ on ${\rm SO}(3)\cong{\rm PSU}(2) \cong \R P^3$ such that $\int_{\R P^3} v_{ \R P^3}=1/2.$
\end{lem}

\begin{proof}
The naturality of the construction in Definition~\ref{def:betaM} shows that for each
$n\ge1$, the restriction $i_n^*(\beta_M)$ is a ${\rm PSU}(n+1)$-invariant Lie algebra
$3$-cocycle on $\mathfrak{psu}(n+1)$.
Since $\mathfrak{psu}(n+1)$ is simple, $H^3_{\rm GF}(\mathfrak{psu}(n+1);\R)\cong\R$ and
every ${\rm PSU}(n+1)$-invariant $3$-cocycle is a scalar multiple of the Cartan
$3$-cocycle (see \eqref{phiphi} for the definition).

Thus, by functoriality, it suffices to show the latter claim with $n=1.$
Via the identification $\C P^1 \cong S^2 \subset \R^3$, we may view ${\rm PSU}(2)$ as
${\rm SO}(3)$.
Let $
 x,y,z : S^2\to\R
$
be the coordinate functions; they satisfy $\int_{S^2}x\,\omega_1 = \int_{S^2}y\,\omega_1 =
\int_{S^2}z\,\omega_1 =0$. 
Let $X_x,X_y,X_z$ be the corresponding Hamiltonian vector fields.
The Poisson bracket relations are
\[
  \{x,y\}=z,\qquad
  \{y,z\}=x,\qquad
  \{z,x\}=y,
\]
so $X_x,X_y,X_z$ form a standard basis of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$.
Notice by the nomarization $\int_{S^2} \omega_1 = 2\pi$, the radious of $S^2$ may be $1/2$;  
Using Definition~\ref{def:betaM} we compute
\[
\begin{aligned}
  i^*_1 \bigl(\beta_{\C P^1}(X_x,X_y,X_z)\bigr)
   &= \frac{3}{\pi^3 } \int_{S^2} x\,\{y,z\} \omega_1= \frac{1}{\pi^3 } \int_{S^2} \bigl(x\,\{y,z\} +  y\,\{z,x\} +z\,\{x,y\} \bigr)\,\omega_1 \\ 
  = \frac{1}{\pi^3 }\int_{S^2} (x^2+y^2+z^2)\,\omega_1   &=  \frac{1}{4\pi^3 }  \int_{S^2} \omega_1   =\frac{1}{2 \pi^2 }   \neq 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here, by the normalization $ \int_{S^2} \omega_1 =2 \pi $ and the volume of $S^2$ is $4\pi$, we should notice $ x^2+y^2+z^2= 1/4$.
Since $i_1^*(\beta_M)$ is $\SO(3)$-invariant and $\AAA^3(\R P^3 )^{\SO(3)} \cong \R$, 
$i_1^*(\beta_M)$ is a nonzero multiple of $v_{ \R P^3}$. Hence, since $ v_{ \R P^3}(X_x,X_y,X_z)= 1/2\pi^2 $ by definition, 
we have the required $ i_1^*(\beta_M) = v_{ \R P^3} $.
\end{proof}

We now recall two facts about symplectomorphism groups.
First, when $M=\C P^n$ and $n=1,2$, the inclusion $
 {\rm PSU}(n+1)\subset \Diff_{\omega_n}(\C P^n)$
is a homotopy equivalence: for $n=1$ this is the classical Smale conjecture, and for
$n=2$ it is due to Gromov \cite{Gro}. Here, we should refer to $\pi_1({\rm PSU}(n))\cong \Z/n $.
For $n>2$ no analogous result is presently known.

Second, for the product $(\C P^1 \times\C P^1 ,\omega_1 \oplus\omega_1)$ there is a homotopy equivalence
\begin{equation}\label{homotopy1}
\bigl(\SO(3)\times \SO(3)\bigr)\rtimes \mathbb{Z}/2  \;\simeq\; \Diff_{\omega_1 \oplus\omega_1}(S^2\times S^2) \cong \Diff_{\omega_1 \oplus\omega_1,0}(S^2\times S^2) \rtimes \Z/2
\end{equation}
(see \cite{AM}). Here, the left equivalence is induced from the inclusion.
 \begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem \ref{main3}]
Let $M$ be one of $\C P^1$, $\C P^2$ or $\C P^1\times\C P^1$ with the symplectic form $\omega$ in the statement,
and let $\GG\to \Diff_{\omega,0}(M)$ be the universal covering group.
In each case we have $\pi_2(\Diff_{\omega,0}(M))=0$ as mentioned above, hence $\GG$ is $2$--connected.
Fix a convex chart and $U\subset \GG$ as in Subsection~\ref{sec223344}.
Then Lemma~\ref{key3} (with $q=3$) provides a well-configured sequence of length $3$ and a filling $\sigma$ over $\Lambda=\Z$,
and Proposition~\ref{444} applied to $\lambda=\beta_M$ yields a locally smooth 3-cocycle
$\mathcal{F}_{\sigma}(\beta_M)\in Z^3_{\Delta}(\GG;\R/\Z).$

\smallskip\noindent
\textbf{Case 1: $M=\C P^1$ or $\C P^2$.}
Let $\tilde\iota:\SU(2)\to \GG$ be the lift of the standard inclusion
$\SU(2)\subset \SU(n+1)\twoheadrightarrow{\rm PSU}(n+1)\subset \Diff_{\omega_n}(\C P^n)$ ($n=1,2$).
By Lemma~\ref{ddddd} (and naturality), $\tilde\iota^*(\beta_M)$ is a nonzero integral multiple of the bi-invariant generator on $\SU(2)$;
hence the pullback $\tilde\iota^*[\mathcal{F}_{\sigma}(\beta_M)]\in H^3_{\rm gr}(\SU(2);\R/\Z)$ is the twice of the CCS class (Theorem~\ref{tsukau}),
where the twice is obtained by varification with Lemma \ref{ddddd} and Theorem \ref{tsukau}.
Therefore, for every $m$ one can choose a homomorphism $j_m:\Z/m\to\SU(2)$ with
a generator $ \tau_m\in H^{\rm gr}_3(\Z/m;\Z)$ satisfying
\[
\bigl\langle (\tilde\iota\circ j_m)^*[\mathcal{F}_{\sigma}(\beta_M)],\tau_m\bigr\rangle=[4/m]\in \Q/\Z
\qquad(\text{cf. }\cite[\S\,1.3]{DZ}),
\]
where $\tau_m$ generates $H_3(\Z/m)\cong \Z/m$.
Applying Lemma~\ref{321a}\textup{(iii)} to the covering $\GG\to \Diff_{\omega,0}(M)$ gives
$\Q/\Z\subset H_3^{\rm gr}(\Diff_{\omega,0}(M))$, hence $\Q/\Z\subset H_3^{\rm gr}(\Diff_{\omega_n}(\C P^n))$.

\smallskip\noindent
\textbf{Case 2: $M=\C P^1\times\C P^1$ and $\omega=\omega_1\oplus\omega_1$.}
The diagonal embedding $\delta:\Diff_{\omega_1}(\C P^1)\to \Diff_{\omega,0}(M)$, $f\mapsto(f\times f)$,
pulls back $\beta_M$ to a nonzero multiple of $\beta_{\C P^1}$; restricting further to the diagonal $\SU(2)$ reduces to Case~1,
and yields $\Q/\Z\subset H_3^{\rm gr}(\Diff_{\omega,0}(M))$.
Finally, \eqref{homotopy1} gives $\Diff_{\omega}(M)\cong \Diff_{\omega,0}(M)\rtimes \Z/2$,
and the induced class is $\Z/2$--invariant (the swap map preserves $\omega$ and hence $\beta_M$);
thus Lemma~\ref{321a}\textup{(ii)} implies $\Q/\Z\subset H_3^{\rm gr}(\Diff_{\omega}(M))$.
\end{proof}

Combining this with Proposition~\ref{444} gives the following consequence, which may be
viewed as a partial answer to a question raised in \cite[\S\,2]{Rez2}.

whose restriction to ${\rm PSU}(n+1)$ coincides (up to a nonzero scalar) with the
Cheeger--Chern--Simons cocycle of ${\rm PSU}(n+1)$ explained in Example \ref{ex2344}.

\section{Applications to the smooth cohomology of $\Diff_v(M)$}\label{sec2233}

The goal of this section is to prove Theorem~\ref{main1}.
The key ingredient will be the Chern--Simons invariant, which we briefly review in
Subsection~\ref{sssdd}.
In Subsection~\ref{sec3a884}, we give the proof of Theorem \ref{main1}, and in Section \ref{hyp11}, we similarly discuss hyperbolic case.
Finally, in Section \ref{sec293392}, 
we discuss obstruction of smoothness of cocycles on $\Ss\neq\{G^{n+1}\}$. 
\subsection{Review: Cheeger--Chern--Simons cocycles}\label{sssdd}

We begin by recalling the definition of the Chern--Simons form.
Let $G$ be a Lie group with Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, and let
$E\to M$ be a principal $G$-bundle.
Let $  P\colon\mathfrak g^k\to\R$
be a symmetric $k$-linear map which is invariant under the diagonal adjoint action
$G\curvearrowright\mathfrak g^k$.
Let $t \in \R.$
Given two connections $\omega_0,\omega_1\in\AAA^1(E;\mathfrak g)$, we consider the
affine interpolation
$
 \omega_t:=(1- t)\,\omega_0 + t\,\omega_1$
and denote by
$
 \Omega_t:=d\omega_t+\tfrac12[\omega_t,\omega_t]$ its curvature.
By the basic results of Chern--Weil theory, the $2k$-form
$P(\Omega_t,\dots,\Omega_t)$ is closed and its de Rham cohomology class is independent of $t$.
The \emph{Chern--Simons $(2k-1)$-form} associated with $P$ and the pair of connections 
$\omega_0,\omega_1$ is defined by
\[
  T_P(\omega_0,\omega_1)
  :=k\int_0^1 P\bigl(\omega_0 -\omega_1,\Omega_t,\dots,\Omega_t\bigr)\,dt
  \in\Omega^{2k-1}(M).
\]
It satisfies the transgression identity
\[
  P(\Omega_0,\dots,\Omega_0)-P(\Omega_1,\dots,\Omega_1)
  =d\bigl( T_P(\omega_0,\omega_1)\bigr).
\]

If $M$ is a closed $(2k-1)$-dimensional manifold, the (relative) \emph{Chern--Simons invariant} for two connections $\omega_0,\omega_1$ is
the integral $
 \int_M T_P(\omega_0,\omega_1) \in \R$. 

There are two natural issues here.
First, this integral is in general not gauge invariant.
However, for suitable normalizations of $P$, the integral $ \int_M T_P(\omega_0,\omega_1) \in \R/\Z$ modulo $\Z$ is often well
defined and becomes gauge invariant. 
Second, one has to choose the reference connection $\omega_0$.
Two standard choices are the following:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item If $E$ is the trivial bundle $G\times M$, one often takes $\omega_0$ to be the
      trivial connection.
\item If $G=\SO(2k-1)$ and $E$ is the principal frame bundle associated with the tangent
      bundle of $M$, one takes $\omega_0$ to be the Levi-Civita connection of a fixed
      Riemannian metric on $M$.
\end{enumerate}

Next, we recall the notion of \emph{Cheeger--Chern--Simons cocycles} (CCS cocycles);
see \cite{CS}.
For each group $G$ endowed with the discrete topology we fix an Eilenberg--MacLane space
$K(G,1)$.
If $G=\pi_1(M)$, we fix a classifying map $
 \iota: M \ra K(\pi_1(M),1).$
Given a group homomorphism $f:\pi_1(M)\to G$, there is an induced cellular map
$f_*\circ\iota :M \to K(G,1)$, unique up to homotopy.
In particular, the fundamental class $[M]\in H_{2k-1}(M )$ has a well-defined image
\[
 f_*[M]\in H_{2k-1}(K(G,1) )\cong H_{2k-1}^{\rm gr}(G ).
\]
On the other hand, the basic theory of flat bundles associates to $f$ a principal
$G$-bundle $E_f\to M$ endowed with a flat connection $\omega_f$, up to conjugacy.

In the above situation, a group $(2k-1)$-cocycle $c_P^{\mathrm{CS}}: G^{2k} \to \R/\Z$ is called a
\emph{Cheeger--Chern--Simons cocycle} \cite{CS} for $P$ if for every group homomorphism
$f:\pi_1(M)\to G$ there exists a connection $\omega_0$ on $E_f$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{csinv}
  \int_M T_P (\omega_0,\omega_f) 
  = \bigl\langle [c_P^{\mathrm{CS}}], f_* [M]\bigr\rangle
  \in\R/\Z.
\end{equation}
In situations (i) and (ii) above, the reference connection $\omega_0$ is chosen as
indicated: trivial in case~(i) and Levi-Civita in case~(ii), respectively.

In general, the existence of CCS cocycles depends on the choice of $E$, $G$ and $P$, and
even when they exist it is a subtle problem to decide on which subset $S_{2k-1} \subset G^{2k}$ such a
cocycle can be chosen to be smooth.
The history of this problem is long and intricate, so we confine ourselves to quoting two
typical results, which we use later.
\begin{exa}\label{ex21}
Let $k=2n$ and $G={\rm SO}(4n)$, and let $P$ be the $n$-th Pontryagin polynomial.
Set $K:= {\rm SO}(4n-1)$; then $G/K\cong S^{4n-1}$.
Let $\lambda$ denote the standard volume form ${\rm vol}(S^{4n-1})$ on $S^{4n-1}$.
By Proposition~\ref{312} we can construct a filling $\sigma$ and obtain a
group cocycle $ \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}\bigl({\rm vol}(S^{4n-1})\bigr) : G^{4n} \ra \R/\Z.$
According to \cite{DK,Dup3}, this cocycle is a CCS cocycle associated with $P$.
Moreover, the restriction 
to the well-configured sequence $ S^{*}_{\rm hem}$ in Example~\ref{i1255},
is smooth by definition.
\end{exa}
\begin{exa}\label{ex23}
Let $G={\rm SL}_n(\C)$ or $G=\SU(n)$, and let $P$ be the polynomial corresponding to the
second Chern class, namely $P(A,B)=\frac{1}{2\pi^2}\mathrm{Tr}(AB)$. 
If $\dim M=3$, obstruction theory implies that every principal $G$-bundle over $M$ is trivial; it is natural to take $\omega_0$ to be the trivial connection.
In addition, we review a known result: 
\begin{thm}\label{tsukau}Let $\lambda$ be $(1/24 \pi ^2)\Tr ( \omega_{\rm CM} \wedge\omega_{\rm CM} \wedge\omega_{\rm CM} )$ as a $G$-invariant $3$-form on $G$,
where $\omega_{\rm CM} \in \AAA^1 (G;\g)$ is the Maurer--Cartan 1-form.
By the $2$-connectivity of $G$, considering the sequence $\{ S_*^{\neq h}\}$ introduced in \eqref{989796}, 
and an appropriate filling $ \sigma$ from Proposition \ref{312}, 
the $3$-cocycle $
 \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}(\lambda) : G^4 \ra \C/\Z$
is a CCS cocycle $ c_P^{\mathrm{CS}} $. Moreover, if $ G=\SL_2 (\C)$, then $
 \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}(\lambda)$ 
is smooth on $S_3^{\neq h} $, and if $G=\SU(2)$, the image of $c_P^{\mathrm{CS}}$ lies in $\R/\Z\subset\C/\Z$.
\end{thm}
The construction is due to some papers \cite{DZ,Dup3,Zic} etc, where deep connections with the
dilogarithm and the extended Bloch group are also developed; we do not recall the details
here.
\end{exa}
\subsection{A lemma on transfer}\label{sec3a4}

In several places we use a basic lemma \ref{321a} below concerning transfer in group cohomology.
For the reader's convenience we include a proof.
Let $\Gamma$ be a group and let $G\subset \Gamma$ be a normal subgroup of finite index $| \Gamma/G| <\infty$.
Let $A$ be either $\R$ or $\R/\Z$, regarded as a trivial $\Gamma$-module.

We review the transfer (corestriction) on homogeneous cochains from \cite[Chapter 4]{Bro}.
Choose a set $T\subset \Gamma$ of representatives for the \emph{right} cosets $G\backslash\Gamma$;
thus $\Gamma=\bigsqcup_{t\in T}Gt$ and we may assume $e\in T$.
For $t\in T$ and $\gamma\in \Gamma$ let $\overline{t\gamma}\in T$ be the unique representative of the right coset $G(t\gamma)$. 
For $\phi \in C^n_{\Delta}(G;A)$ we define a cochain $\Tr(\phi)\in C^n_{\Delta}(\Gamma;A)$ by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:transfer-def}
\Tr(\phi)(\gamma_0,\ldots,\gamma_n)
:=\sum_{t\in T}\phi\bigl((t\gamma_0) \overline{t\gamma_0}^{-1}, (t\gamma_1 ) \overline{t\gamma_1}^{-1} , \ldots, (t\gamma_n ) \overline{t\gamma_n }^{-1} \bigr).
\end{equation}
Then, the map $\Tr:\ C^*_{\Delta}(G;A)^{G}\longrightarrow C^*_{\Delta}(\Gamma;A)^{\Gamma}$ is known to be 
a chain map, which is the usual transfer (corestriction) for the inclusion $j: G\hookrightarrow  \Gamma$.
Notice that the quotient $\Gamma/G$ acts on $G$ by conjugation,this induces an action of $\Gamma/G$ on $H^*_{\rm gr}(G;A)$.
If a cocycle $\phi$ is invariant under the action, we have $j^* \circ  \Tr([\phi])=|B|\,[\phi]$ by definition.

If $\Gamma$ is a (Fr\'echet) Lie group and $G\subset \Gamma$ is an \emph{open} subgroup of finite index, then each right coset $Gt$ is open and closed.
In this case, for each fixed $t\in T$ the maps $\gamma\mapsto \overline{t\gamma}$ and $\gamma\mapsto t\gamma\,\overline{t\gamma}^{-1}$ are locally smooth on $Gt$,
and \eqref{eq:transfer-def} restricts to chain maps
\[
\Tr:\ C^*_{\rm sm}(G;A)^{G}\to C^*_{\rm sm}(\Gamma;A)^{\Gamma},
\qquad
\Tr:\ C^*_{\rm loc,sm}(G;A)^{G}\to C^*_{\rm loc,sm}(\Gamma;A)^{\Gamma}.
\]

\begin{lem}\label{321a}
Assume that $n$ is odd.
Let $\Gamma$ be a group and let $G\triangleleft \Gamma$ be a normal subgroup of finite index, and set $B:=\Gamma/G$.
Let $\phi\in Z^n_{\Delta}(G;\R/\Z)^{G}$ be a group $n$-cocycle which is invariant under the induced action of $B$.
Set $\widetilde{\phi}:=\Tr(\phi)\in Z^n_{\Delta}(\Gamma;\R/\Z)^{\Gamma}$.

\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item The cocycle $\widetilde{\phi}$ satisfies $\widetilde{\phi}|_{G^{n+1}}=|B|\,\phi$, i.e.\ $j^*\widetilde{\phi}=|B|\phi$.
\item Suppose that there exists an integer $c_G\in\N$ with the following property:
      for every $m\in\N$ there exists a group homomorphism
      $\iota_m : \Z/m \to G$ such that the map
      \[
        H_n^{\rm gr}(\Z/m; \Z) \longrightarrow \Q/\Z,
        \qquad
        \kappa \longmapsto \langle \iota_m^* [\phi], \kappa \rangle
      \]
      has image
      $\{ [c_G s/m] \in \Q/\Z \mid s \in \Z\}$.
      Then $H_n^{\rm gr}(\Gamma)$ contains a subgroup isomorphic to $\Q/\Z$.
\item Let $q:\Gamma\to G'$ be a surjective homomorphism whose kernel $K:=\Ker(q)$ is finite and central.
      Then there exists a class $[\phi']\in H^n_{\rm gr}(G';\R/\Z)$ such that
      \[
      q^*[\phi']=|K|\,[\widetilde{\phi}]\in H^n_{\rm gr}(\Gamma;\R/\Z).
      \]
      Moreover, if the hypothesis in \textup{(ii)} holds for $\phi$, then $H_n(G')$ contains a subgroup isomorphic to $\Q/\Z$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lem}
\begin{proof}
\noindent\textbf{(i)} This is explained above.

\noindent\textbf{(ii)}
Let ${\rm ev}:=\langle[\widetilde{\phi}],-\rangle:\Tor H_n^{\rm gr}(\Gamma;\Z)\to \Tor(\R/\Z)=\Q/\Z$.
For each $m$ let $\tau_m\in H_n^{\rm gr}(\Z/m;\Z)\cong\Z/m$ be a generator, set
$\bar\iota_m:=j\circ\iota_m$, and put $x_m:=\bar\iota_{m*}(\tau_m)\in \Tor H_n^{\rm gr}(\Gamma;\Z)$.
Naturality and \textup{(i)} give
\[{
\rm ev}(x_m)=\langle \bar\iota_m^{\,*}[\widetilde{\phi}],\tau_m\rangle
=\langle \iota_m^{\,*}(j^*[\widetilde{\phi}]),\tau_m\rangle
=|B|\langle \iota_m^{\,*}[\phi],\tau_m\rangle \in \Q/\Z.
\]
Hence $\Im({\rm ev})$ contains $\{[|B|c_G s/m]\mid s\in\Z\}$ for every $m$.
Since multiplication by $|B|c_G$ is surjective on $\Q/\Z$, we get $\Im({ \rm ev})=\Q/\Z$.
Thus $\Tor H_n^{\rm gr}(\Gamma;\Z)\twoheadrightarrow\Q/\Z$; as $\Q/\Z$ is divisible (hence injective),
this surjection splits and $\Q/\Z$ embeds into $H_n^{\rm gr}(\Gamma)$.

\noindent\textbf{(iii)}
Since $K$ is finite, $H^q_{\rm gr}(K;\R/\Z)$ is $|K|$-torsion for $q>0$.
Hence the inflation map $q^*:H^n_{\rm gr} (G';\R/\Z)\to H^n_{\rm gr}(\Gamma;\R/\Z)$ has cokernel annihilated by $|K|$
(e.g.\ by the Lyndon--Hochschild--Serre spectral sequence).
Therefore $|K|[\widetilde{\phi}]\in \mathrm{Im}(q^*)$, so we can choose $[\phi']\in H^n_{\rm gr}(G';\R/\Z)$ with
$q^*[\phi']=|K|\,[\widetilde{\phi}]$.

Assume moreover the hypothesis in \textup{(ii)}.
Set $\mathrm{ev}_{\Gamma}:=\langle[\widetilde{\phi}],-\rangle:\Tor H_n^{\rm gr}(\Gamma;\Z)\to\Q/\Z$
and $\mathrm{ev}_{G'}:=\langle[\phi'],-\rangle:\Tor H_n^{\rm gr}(G';\Z)\to\Q/\Z$.
Then for any $x\in \Tor H_n^{\rm gr}(\Gamma;\Z)$ we have
\[
\mathrm{ev}_{G'}(q_*x)=\langle[\phi'],q_*x\rangle=\langle q^*[\phi'],x\rangle
=|K|\langle[\widetilde{\phi}],x\rangle=|K|\mathrm{ev}_{\Gamma}(x).
\]
By \textup{(ii)} the map $\mathrm{ev}_{\Gamma}$ is surjective, and multiplication by $|K|$ is surjective on $\Q/\Z$,
hence $\mathrm{ev}_{G'}$ is surjective.
Since $\Q/\Z$ is divisible, the surjection $\Tor H_n(G';\Z)\twoheadrightarrow \Q/\Z$ splits, and therefore
$\Q/\Z$ embeds into $H_n^{\rm gr}(G')$.
\end{proof}

\begin{thm}\label{main3}
Let ${\Bbb C} P^n$ be equipped with the symplectic $2$-form $\ww_n$ arising from the Fubini--Study metric.
Then the third group homology with integer coefficients of each of the following groups
contains a subgroup isomorphic to ${\Bbb Q}/{\Bbb Z}$:
\[
\Diff_{\ww_1}({\Bbb C} P^1),\qquad
\Diff_{\ww_1\times \ww_1}({\Bbb C} P^1\times {\Bbb C} P^1),\qquad
\Diff_{\ww_2}({\Bbb C} P^2).
\]
\end{thm}

\begin{thm}\label{main4}
Let $\alpha_{\rm st}\in{\cal A}^1(S^3)$ be the standard contact 1-form on the $3$-sphere $S^3$
(defining the standard contact structure $\ker(\alpha_{\rm st})$).
Then $H_3^{\rm gr}\bigl(\Diff_{\alpha_{\rm st}}(S^3)\bigr)$ contains a subgroup isomorphic to ${\Bbb Q}/{\Bbb Z}$.
\end{thm}

\noindent\textbf{Ideas of the proof.}
Compared with much of the existing literature on degree-three classes for diffeomorphism groups,
our results are formulated at the (locally) cocycle level. In fact, 
The key step is the construction of a nontrivial locally smooth ${\Bbb R}/{\Bbb Z}$-valued group $3$-cocycle
of Chern--Simons type \cite{CS}.
Starting from an invariant differential form $\lambda$ on a (Fr\'echet) Lie group ${\cal G}$,
we construct a cochain by integrating $\lambda$ over a family of simplices with prescribed vertices
(Section~\ref{sec33233}).
In infinite dimensions such a straightening is not available canonically on the full Cartesian power
${\cal G}^{n+1}$, and even in finite dimensions one typically obtains smoothness only on suitable open subsets.
To organize this systematically, we work in the restriction-of-domain framework of Definition~\ref{asfa}:
we replace the full homogeneous complex by an invariant subcomplex ${\Bbb Z}\langle S_*\rangle$
coming from a \emph{well-configured} sequence ${\cal S}=\{S_n\subset {\cal G}^{n+1}\}$
(Section~\ref{sec2d991}).

For the diffeomorphism groups considered here, we take $S_n$ to be the set of \emph{$U$-small tuples}
$(g_0,\dots,g_n)$ for which all relative differences $g_i^{-1}g_j$ lie in a fixed identity neighbourhood $U$
(Definition~\eqref{def:U-small}).
A fixed convex chart around the identity then yields an explicit \emph{affine straightening}:
using an ``affine join'' inside the chart we construct a filling $\sigma$ over $\Ss_{{\cal G},U}$
(Subsection~\ref{sec223344}) and hence a cochain $\mathcal{F}_{\sigma}(\lambda): {\cal G}^{n+1} \rightarrow {\Bbb R}/{\Bbb Z}$ by integration.
To obtain an honest ${\Bbb R}/{\Bbb Z}$-valued cocycle, one must control periods and, crucially, eliminate the
low-degree homotopy obstruction encoded in Proposition~\ref{baas} (notably involving $\pi_2({\cal G} )$).
In the groups in the theorems, this obstruction can be verified to vanish using concrete homotopy-type results:
in the $3$-manifold cases we use Smale-type theorems identifying
$\Diff_v (M)$ with the isometry group $\mathrm{Isom}^+(M)$---namely the generalized Smale conjecture proved by Bamler--Kleiner
for spherical space forms \cite{BK}, and Gabai's theorem in the hyperbolic case \cite{Gabai}.
Finally, Proposition~\ref{43333} shows that the derivation of the cocycle $\mathcal{F}_{\sigma}(\lambda)$ 
is a representative cocycle in the
Gel'fand--Fuks cohomology of the Lie algebra of $\Diff_\lambda (M) $.
This compatibility is the main tool for detecting nontriviality by restriction to compact subgroups and
comparison with classical Cheeger--Chern--Simons classes (see Section \ref{sec2233} and ~\ref{sssdd} or \cite{DPS,DZ}).

This idea yields new and computable $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$-torsion phenomena in $H^{\mathrm{gr}}_{3}$
for several classical diffeomorphism groups arising in low-dimensional and symplectic-contact topology.
In fact, for symplectic manifolds, we use known homotopy equivalences for ${\Bbb C} P^1$ and the results of Gromov
for ${\Bbb C} P^2$ \cite{Gro} and Abreu--McDuff for $({\Bbb C} P^1\times{\Bbb C} P^1,\omega_1\oplus\omega_1)$ \cite{AM},
which again imply the required vanishing of $\pi_2$ in the identity component; 
Theorems \ref{main3}--\ref{main4} follow by applying the ideas presented above.
Incidentally, the hyperbolic case (Section~\ref{hyp11}) yields a related ${\Bbb R}$-valued $3$-cocycle whose
vanishing in cohomology remains open.

\noindent\textbf{Organization of the paper.}
Section~\ref{sec299} fixes conventions on (locally smooth) group (co)homology,
the restriction-of-domain method, and well-configured complexes.
Section~\ref{sec33233} adapts Dupont's straightening framework \cite{Dup1,Dup2,Dup3} to well-configured complexes.
Section~\ref{sec2233} reviews Cheeger--Chern--Simons theory and proves Theorem~\ref{main1};
the hyperbolic case is discussed in Section~\ref{hyp11}.
Section~\ref{sec32884} treats symplectic manifolds and proves Theorem~\ref{main3}.
Finally, Section~\ref{sec32d} deals with contact manifolds and proves Theorem~\ref{main4}.

\noindent\textbf{Conventions.}
Throughout, ${\cal G}$ denotes a topological group with identity element $e$.
Unless stated otherwise, manifolds are connected, closed, oriented, and smooth.

\begin{equation}
(u,\upsilon)_{L^2}=\int_{\Omega}u\upsilon d\gamma,\quad \forall\, u,\upsilon\in L^2(\Omega,\gamma).
\end{equation}
By the weighted Poincar\'{e} inequality, the associated scalar product of the Hilbert space $W^{1,2}_0(\Omega,d\gamma)$ can be given as
\[
(u,\upsilon)_{W_0^{1,2}}=\int_{\Omega}\nabla u\cdot \nabla \upsilon d\gamma,\quad \mathrm{for\ any}\ u,\upsilon\in W^{1,2}_0(\Omega,\gamma).
\]

The spaces $W^{1,2}(\Omega,\gamma)$ and $W^{2,2}(\Omega,\gamma)$ are defined in a similar way. These Sobolev spaces are all separable Hilbert spaces with respect to the Gaussian measure (see for instance \cite{Tero1994,Radulescu2019} and references therein). When $\Omega$ is bounded the density function $e^{-|x|^2/2}$ has positive upper and lower bounds in $\Omega$, hence it is obvious that $L^2(\Omega,\gamma)=L^2(\Omega)$, $W^{1,2}(\Omega,\gamma)=W^{1,2}(\Omega)$, and so on. However, we only have $W^{1,2}(\Omega)\subset W^{1,2}(\Omega,\gamma)$ and $W^{1,2}_0(\Omega)\subset W^{1,2}_0(\Omega,\gamma)$ when $\Omega$ is unbounded.

\subsection{The Ornstein-Unlenbeck operator and its spectrum}\label{Se2-1}

Let $\Omega$ be an open subset of $\R^n$. The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator $L_\Omega$ relative to $\Omega$, is defined as follows
\[
L_\Omega u=\Delta u-(x,\nabla u).
\]
It will be important to identify the domain of this operator. When $\Omega=\R^n$, we set
$$
\text{Dom}(L_{\R^n}):=W^{2,2}(\R^n,\gamma).
$$
For a general open set $\Omega$, we just note now that $L_\Omega$ is well defined on $W^{2,2}(\Omega,\gamma)$; later on we restrict $L_\Omega$ to a slightly different space of functions.

Integration by parts shows that $L_\Omega$ is self-adjoint with respect to the Gaussian measure, in the following sense: for every $\phi,\psi \in C_{c}^\infty (\Omega)$,
\[
\int_{\Omega} \phi L_\Omega\psi d\gamma=-\int_{\Omega} (\nabla \phi, \nabla \psi)d\gamma=\int_{\Omega} \psi L_\Omega\phi d\gamma.
\]

\medskip

For an open bounded set $\Omega\subset\R^n$, with Lipschitz boundary, it is well-known (and it follows via, say, a variational argument), that there exists a unique positive number $\lambda_{\gamma}(\Omega)$ such that the boundary value problem \eqref{Lambda-Gauss-intro}
admits a solution $u\in W^{1,2}_0(\Omega,\gamma)$. Moreover, the solution is unique up to multiplication by positive constants (see \cite[Theorem 2.1]{CFLS24}). When no ambiguity may arise, we will write $\lambda_\gamma$ instead of $ \lambda_\gamma(\Omega)$.

In view of the previous definition, $\lambda_\gamma$ is an eigenvalue of the operator $L_\Omega$. By standard spectral theory (see \cite[Theorem 4.46]{Arendt-Urban2023}), the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator has, more generally, a countable set of eigenvalues $\Sigma=\{\lambda_i\in \R^{+}| 0<\lambda_\gamma=\lambda_1<\lambda_2\leq \cdots \leq \lambda_k\leq\cdots \}$, with $\lambda_k\rightarrow +\infty\ \text{as}\ k\rightarrow +\infty$, whose normalized eigenfunctions $\{ \phi_k\}$ are mutually orthogonal and span $W^{1,2}_0(\Omega,\gamma)$ (in $L^2(\Omega,\gamma)$ as well). By the regularity theory of elliptic partial differential equations, $\phi_k \in C^{\infty}(\Omega)\cap C^0(\overline{\Omega})$ for every $k$ (cf. \cite{Evans}).

\section{The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup and the Trotter product formula}\label{Se3}

In this section we show that, if $\Omega$ is a bounded open set with Lipschitz boundary, the semigroup generated by $L_\Omega$ can be obtained from the semigroup relative to $L_{\R^n}$ via Trotter product formula. Our general references for the theory of semigroups are \cite{Arendt-handbook,Pazy1983}.

Let $(P_\gamma(t))_{t\geq 0}$ be the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup with generator operator $-L_{\R^n}$. It is well-known (see for instance \cite{Book-Markov-Diffu}) that $P_\gamma(t)$ admits a kernel density, called Mehler kernel, with respect to the Lebesgue measure in $\R^n$. This means that there exists a function $p=p(x,z;t)$, with $x,z\in\R^n$, and $t>0$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{Pf}
[P_\gamma(t)f](x)=\int_{\R^n}p(x,z,t)f(z)dz\,,
\end{equation}

\section{Application to the first eigenfunction of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator}\label{Se5}

In this section, we give new proofs to Theorems \ref{Application1} and \ref{Application2}.

Let $\Omega$ be a bounded open subset of $\R^n$, with Lipschitz boundary, and $u$ be a solution of \eqref{Lambda-Gauss-intro}. This is equivalent to say that $\lambda_\gamma=\lambda_1$ is the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of the operator $-L$ in $\Omega$, and $u=\phi_1$ is the corresponding first eigenfunction.

\begin{proof}[\bf Proof of Theorem \ref{Application1}]
We will prove that
$$
\lim_{t\to+\infty}p_\gamma^{\Omega}(x,z;t)e^{\lambda_1 t}e^{-|z|^2/2}=u(x)u(z)e^{-|z|^2/2}
$$
for every $x,z\in\Omega$. By Theorem \ref{Lemma-1}, this implies that $u$ is log-concave. The previous relation is equivalent to prove that
$$
\lim_{t\to+\infty}p_\gamma^{\Omega}(x,z;t)e^{\lambda_1 t}=u(x)u(z)
$$
for every $x,z\in\Omega$. By \eqref{aggiunta 1000},
\[
p^{\Omega}_\gamma\cdot e^{\lambda_1 t}-u(x)u(z)=\mathop{\sum}_{k=2}^{\infty} e^{(-\lambda_k+\lambda_1) t} \phi_{k}(x)\phi_{k}(z), \quad\forall\,(x,z)\in\Omega\times\Omega,\, \forall\, t>0.
\]
By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,
\begin{align*}
|p^\Omega_{\gamma}(x,z;t)&\cdot e^{\lambda_1t}-u(x)u(z)|\\
&\leq  \left( \mathop{\sum}_{k=2}^{\infty}  e^{(-\lambda_k +\lambda_1) t}\phi^2_{k}(x) \right)^{1/2} \left( \mathop{\sum}_{k=2}^{\infty}  e^{(-\lambda_k +\lambda_1) t}\phi^2_{k}(z) \right)^{1/2} .
\end{align*}
In order to get bounds on each of these square roots, we use again the spectral representation with $z=x$ and $t=1$, and Proposition \ref{p2}:
\begin{equation}\label{Kac-(9.9)}
\mathop{\sum}_{k=1}^{\infty}  e^{-\lambda_k }\phi^2_{k}(x)=p^\Omega_{\gamma}(x,x;1)\leq c_0 (1-e^{-2})^{-n/2},
\end{equation}
where the positive constant $c_0$ depends on $\Omega$ and $n$. For $t>0$, we define $M(t):=\sup_{k\geq 2}e^{-\lambda_kt+\lambda_1t+\lambda_k}$, we have
\begin{align*}
|p_{\gamma}^{\Omega}(x,z;t)&\cdot e^{\lambda_1t}-u(x)u(z)|\\
&\leq  M(t)\left( \mathop{\sum}_{k=2}^{\infty}  e^{-\lambda_k }\phi^2_{k}(x) \right)^{1/2} \left( \mathop{\sum}_{k=2}^{\infty} e^{-\lambda_k  }\phi^2_{k}(z) \right)^{1/2} \\
&\leq M(t)c_0 (1-e^{-2})^{-n/2}.
\end{align*}
On the other hand, as the sequence $\lambda_k$ is increasing, for $t\ge1$, we have
$$
M(t)\le e^{-\lambda_2t+\lambda_1t+\lambda_2}.
$$
Hence
$$
\lim_{t\rightarrow \infty} M(t)=0.
$$
The proof is completed.
\end{proof}

post_theorem_intro_text:
The starting point for the proof of this results is that the solution $u=u(x,t)$ can be expressed as follows
\begin{equation}\label{1}
u(x,t)= \int_{\Omega}p_{\gamma}^{\Omega} (x,z;t)u_0(z) d\gamma(z)
\end{equation}
(where $\gamma$ is the Gaussian measure). Here $p_\gamma^\Omega$ is the kernel of the parabolic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator, which eventually coincides with the fundamental solution of the equation in \eqref{H-PDE2}, that is, the solution of the following problem:
\begin{equation}\label{parabolic-equation1}
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
& \Delta_x p_\gamma^\Omega(x,z;t)-(x,\nabla_x p_\gamma^\Omega) =\partial_t p_\gamma^\Omega(x,z;t), \quad\forall\ x,z\in\Omega, \ t>0,  \\
& p_\gamma^\Omega(x,z;t)=0, \quad\mbox{if $x\in\partial\Omega$ or $z\in\partial\Omega$, $t>0$},  \\
& p_\gamma^\Omega(x,z;0)d\gamma(z)=\delta(x-z),  \quad  \forall\ x,z\in\Omega,
\end{aligned}
\right.
\end{equation}
where $\delta(x)$ is the Dirac distribution. Very recently, \cite{SUN-Wang2025} proves the partial log-concavity of kernel when $\Omega$ is bounded and convex, that is, fixed $z\in \Omega$ and $t>0$, $p^\Omega_\gamma (x,z;t)$ is log-concave in $x\in \Omega$, and the proof relies on an elliptic method. In the present work, we provide a complete answer through an alternative method.

We point out that, as for the usual heat kernel, although an explicit expression for the entire space $\mathbb R^n$ is well known (see for instance \cite{Book-Markov-Diffu,Evans}),
 no explicit formula for $p_\gamma^\Omega$ is available when $\Omega$ is a generic domain.
However, it was shown in \cite{BL76} that the Trotter product formula can be used to deduce the log-concavity of the usual heat kernel when the domain is open, bounded and convex. Applying the same strategy, we will obtain the log-concavity of the kernel of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck parabolic operator. Precisely, we establish the following theorem, which may be considered in fact the main result of this paper.
\begin{theorem}\label{Lemma-1}
Let $\Omega\subset \mathbb R^n$ be a bounded, convex open set. Then, for every $t>0$, the function
$$
(x,z)\, \rightarrow\,p^\Omega_\gamma (x,z;t) e^{-|z|^2/2},\quad(x,z)\in\Omega\times\Omega
$$
is log-concave.
\end{theorem}
Then, this fact, along with the representation formula \eqref{1}, ensures Theorem \ref{T1}, by a standard argument based on Pr\'ekopa's theorem.

As a consequence of Theorem \ref{T1}, we will obtain new proofs, {\it \`a la} Brascamp and Lieb, of two results established in \cite{CFLS24}: the log-concavity of the first eigenfunction of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator in convex domains and a Brunn-Minkowski type inequality for the relevant eigenvalue. Let us describe in more details these results.

Given an open and bounded set $\Omega$ in $\mathbb R^n$, with Lipschitz boundary, there exists a unique positive number $\lambda_\gamma(\Omega)$, such that the following problem
\begin{equation}\label{Lambda-Gauss-intro}
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
&\Delta u-(x,\nabla u)=-\lambda_\gamma(\Omega) u\quad\mbox{in $\Omega$,}\\\
& u>0\quad\mbox{in $\Omega$,}\\
& u=0\quad\mbox{on $\partial \Omega$},
\end{aligned}
\right.
\end{equation}
admits a solution. $\lambda_\gamma(\Omega)$ is called the first eigenvalue of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator and can be also characterized as follows,
$$
\lambda_\gamma(\Omega)=\inf\left\{\frac{\int_\Omega |\nabla v|^2d\gamma}{\int_\Omega v^2d\gamma}\,: v\in W_0^{1,2}(\Omega),\, v\not\equiv 0\right\}\,,
$$
where $d\gamma$ stands for integration with respect to the Gauss measure $\gamma$, defined as
$$
\gamma(A)=\frac1{(2\pi)^{n/2}}\int_A e^{-|x|^2/2}\mbox{\rm d} x.
$$
The solution of problem \eqref{Lambda-Gauss-intro} is unique up to the multiplication by a (positive) number, and it is called eigenfunction of the eigenvalue $\lambda_\gamma(\Omega)$.
Similarly to the case of the Laplace operator, we can reprove the two following properties.

\begin{theorem}[Theorem 1.2 in \cite{CFLS24}]\label{Application2} Let $s\in [0,1]$. Let $\Omega_0$, $\Omega_1$, and
\[
\Omega_s=(1-s)\Omega_0+s\Omega_1:=\{(1-s)x_0+sx_1:\ x_0\in \Omega_0,\ x_1\in \Omega_1\}
\]
be open bounded subsets of $\mathbb R^n$, $(n\geq 2)$, with Lipschitz boundary. Then
\[
\lambda_\gamma(\Omega_s)\leq (1-s)\lambda_\gamma(\Omega_0)+s\lambda_\gamma(\Omega_1).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Theorem 1.7 in \cite{CFLS24}]\label{Application1}
Let $\Omega$ be an open bounded and convex subset of $\mathbb R^n$. Let $u$ be a solution of problem \eqref{Lambda-Gauss-intro}. Then $u$ is log-concave in $\Omega$.
\end{theorem}

We mention that in \cite{CFLS24} the authors provide two proofs of the previous result, one based on the {\it log-concave envelope}, and another one based on the {\it constant rank theorem} (see also \cite{CCLaMP,Colesanti2025,LeiQin2025} for related topics).

\medskip

The organization of the paper is as follows. In Section \ref{Se2}, we list some basic facts and introduce some notations. In Section \ref{Se3}, we introduce the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup and the Trotter product formula. In Section \ref{Se4}, we give the proof of  Theorem \ref{Lemma-1} and Theorem \ref{T1}. In Section \ref{Se5}, we prove Theorem \ref{Application1} and Theorem \ref{Application2}. In the Appendix, we present the semigroup theory for Ornstein-Uhlebeck in the class of bounded Lipschitz domains.

\medskip
